o: Each operation replaces a subarray by its maximum; we want the longest possible non-decreasing array afterwards. Equivalently, we partition the array into the maximum number of contiguous segments such that the sequence of segment maxima is non-decreasing. Example 1: [4,2,5,3,5] → segments [4],[2,5],[3,5] with maxima [4,5,5] → 3. Example 2 is already sorted → 3. With n up to 2·10⁵ we need roughly linear time.
k: The final array is the sequence of maxima of a partition into contiguous segments.
Greedy stack: when the previous kept value exceeds the current element, merge backwards until order is restored, keeping the merged maximum.

a.i: Process elements left to right with a stack of segment maxima. If the stack top exceeds the incoming value, they cannot coexist in a non-decreasing order; merging the top into the current value (taking the max) is optimal because a larger carried value can only help future comparisons while consuming fewer segments.
s: For each x: while stack top > x, pop and set x = max(x, popped).
Push x; the answer is the final stack size.
a.t: O(n) — each element is pushed and popped at most once.

a.i: Let dp[i] = (length, tail) for the best partition of the prefix ending with a segment that ends at index i. Extend each earlier state dp[j-1] with segment nums[j..i] whose maximum must be ≥ dp[j-1]'s tail; among equal lengths prefer the smaller tail (a smaller tail never hurts future extensions).
s: For each i, scan j from i down to 1 maintaining the running max of nums[j..i].
Take the best (longest, then smallest tail) extension; answer is dp[n].length.
a.t: O(n²) — for each end point we scan all start points.

w: Use the stack solution — it is linear and short. Pitfall: merging the wrong direction (you must fold the popped maximum INTO the incoming element, not push both); equal adjacent values (>) must not be merged. Follow-ups: minimize the number of operations instead (complement counting), or handle a circular array.
